translations.title: Türkiye'den Laredo'ya Ürün Getirme: Hava, Deniz Ve Konsolidasyon
translations.excerpt: Türkiye'den ABD'ye mal getirmenin üç yolu var, ama asıl mesele hangisi değil. Asıl mesele malın iki ayrı gümrükten geçecek olması ve bunu nasıl yöneteceğin.
translations.content:
Türkiye'den Laredo'ya mal hava veya deniz yoluyla gelir; deniz genelde Houston gibi Körfez limanlarına, oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya. Kritik nokta şu: mal ABD'ye girerken bir gümrük işlemi, Meksika'ya geçerken ikinci bir gümrük işlemi görür. Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa bonded depo veya serbest bölge bu iki katmanı yönetmenin yoludur.

  • Türkiye'den ABD'ye üç yol var: hava kargo, deniz konteyneri (LCL veya FCL) ve küçük gönderiler için kurye.
  • Deniz yükü genelde Körfez limanlarına gelir ve oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya taşınır.
  • Mal ABD'ye girerken ABD ithalat işlemi, Meksika'ya geçerken ayrı bir Meksika ithalatı görür.
  • Bonded depoda ABD gümrük vergisi ertelenir; serbest bölgede mal henüz ithal edilmiş sayılmaz.
  • Türkiye menşeli mal T-MEC kapsamında değildir, dolayısıyla Meksika'ya girişte tercihli tarifeden yararlanmaz.

Türkiye'den Laredo depoya ürün nasıl gelir?

Hava veya deniz yoluyla. Hava hızlı ve pahalı, deniz yavaş ve ucuz. Deniz yükü genelde Körfez limanlarına gelir, oradan karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekilir. Küçük gönderiler için kurye de var ama düzenli hacimde birim maliyeti yüksektir.

Türkiye'den Laredo'ya doğrudan bir hat yok, çünkü Laredo bir liman değil kara sınır kapısı. Mal önce ABD'ye giriyor, sonra karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekiliyor. Bunun üç yolu var ve seçim büyük ölçüde aciliyet ile hacim arasındaki dengeye bakıyor. Hava kargo en hızlısı: mal Türkiye'den bir ABD havalimanına uçuyor, gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya geliyor. Numune, ilk parti, sezon yakalama ve yüksek değerli küçük hacimli ürünlerde mantıklı, ama kilogram başına maliyet denizin katları olduğu için düzenli hacimde sürdürülebilir değil. Deniz yolu düzenli hacmin standardı: mal konteynerle Körfez veya Doğu Kıyısı limanlarına geliyor, orada gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya taşınıyor. Houston gibi Körfez limanları Laredo'ya en yakın seçenek olduğu için iç taşıma bacağını kısaltıyor. Deniz tarafında iki alt seçenek var: tam konteyner, yani FCL, ve parsiyel, yani LCL. Hacmin bir konteyneri doldurmuyorsa LCL ile başlarsın; doldurmaya yaklaştığında FCL genelde birim başına daha ucuza gelir. Üçüncü yol kurye, ki numune ve çok küçük gönderiler dışında düzenli iş için uygun değil, çünkü her paket ayrı gümrük görür ve birim maliyet hızla yükselir.

En kritik nokta: mal iki gümrükten geçiyor

Türkiye'den gelen mal ABD'ye girerken bir ithalat, Meksika'ya geçerken ikinci bir ithalat görüyor. Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa, ABD gümrük vergisini kalıcı olarak ödemek gereksiz maliyet olabilir. Bonded depo ve serbest bölge tam bu durum için var.

Bu, Türkiye'den mal getirip Meksika'ya satan herkesin bilmesi gereken ve çoğu içerikte hiç geçmeyen nokta. Malın rotası Türkiye'den Meksika'ya ABD üzerinden geçtiğinde, iki ayrı ülkenin gümrüğüyle iki ayrı kez muhatap oluyorsun. Birincisi ABD'ye giriş: mal ABD'ye ithal ediliyor, sınıflandırılıyor ve Türkiye menşeli olduğu için ABD'nin genel tarife rejimine tabi oluyor. İkincisi Meksika'ya giriş: mal sınırdan geçerken Meksika ithalatı yapılıyor ve orada da Türkiye menşeli olduğu için T-MEC tercihli tarifesinden yararlanamıyor. Yani iki kez gümrük, iki kez evrak. Şimdi asıl soru: malı ABD'de satmayacaksan, ABD gümrük vergisini kalıcı olarak ödemenin bir anlamı var mı? Çoğu durumda yok, ve mevzuat bunun için iki araç sunuyor. Bonded depoda mal ABD gümrük denetimi altında tutulur ve ithalat vergisi mal oradan çıkana kadar ertelenir; mal yeniden ihraç edilirse, yani Meksika'ya gönderilirse, o vergi yükü farklı işler. Serbest bölgede ise mal henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmaz, dolayısıyla oradan Meksika'ya çıkan mal ABD gümrük vergisini hiç doğurmayabilir; ayrıca serbest bölgede etiketleme, kitleme ve montaj gibi katma değerli işlemler yapılabilir. Hangi aracın senin durumuna uyduğu ürüne, hacme ve ne kadar süre bekleteceğine bağlı, o yüzden bunu gümrük müşavirinle konuşmadan rota kurma.

Laredo'da ne yapılır?

Konsolidasyon, hazırlık ve tek ithalat. Farklı tedarikçilerden gelen mal burada birleşir, İspanyolca NOM etiketi vurulur, belgeler hazırlanır ve tek pedimentoyla Meksika'ya geçer. Böylece Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler bölünür.

Laredo'nun rolü bir ara durak olmaktan fazlası; asıl işin yapıldığı yer. Mal buraya ulaştığında dört şey oluyor. Birincisi teslim alma ve sayım: Türkiye'den gelen sevkiyat kontrol ediliyor, eksik veya hasar varsa kaynağa dönmeden tespit ediliyor. İkincisi konsolidasyon: birden fazla tedarikçiden veya birden fazla sevkiyattan gelen mal tek bir ithalat partisinde birleştiriliyor. Bunun neden önemli olduğunu daha önce de yazdık ama tekrar etmeye değer: Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler, yani gümrük müşaviri ücreti, prevalidasyon ve işlem harcı, pedimento başına ödeniyor. Dört ayrı küçük ithalat yapmak yerine tek ithalat yapmak, aynı sabit maliyeti dört kat mala bölüyor. Üçüncüsü hazırlık: Meksika'ya girecek malın İspanyolca NOM etiketi burada vuruluyor, çünkü etiketi menşede veya sınırda basmak, Meksika'da parça başına etiketlemekten her zaman ucuz. Dördüncüsü belge: fatura, çeki listesi ve beyan edilen değer birbiriyle tutarlı hâle getiriliyor, çünkü gümrükte takılmaların çoğu mesafeden değil tutarsız evraktan kaynaklanıyor. Bu dördü tamamlandığında mal tek pedimentoyla geçiyor ve iyi belgelenmiş bir sevkiyat Monterrey'e 1-2 iş gününde ulaşıyor. BringGo Ship'in Laredo deposu tam olarak bu işlevi görüyor, Monterrey deposu da Meksika içi teslimatı ve iadeleri karşılıyor.

Tanımlar

  • LCL: LCL, konteyneri doldurmayan yüklerin başka yüklerle aynı konteyneri paylaştığı parsiyel deniz taşımacılığıdır.
  • Bonded depo: Bonded depo, malın ABD gümrük denetimi altında tutulduğu ve ithalat vergisinin mal çıkana kadar ertelendiği depodur.
  • Serbest bölge (FTZ): Serbest bölge, malın henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmadığı ve katma değerli işlem yapılabilen alandır.

Sık sorulan sorular

Türkiye'den Laredo'ya doğrudan gönderim var mı?

Doğrudan yok, çünkü Laredo bir liman değil kara sınır kapısı. Mal önce hava veya deniz yoluyla ABD'ye giriyor, gümrükleniyor ve karayoluyla Laredo'ya çekiliyor. Deniz yükünde Houston gibi Körfez limanları Laredo'ya en yakın seçenek olduğu için iç taşıma bacağını kısaltıyor.

Hava mı deniz mi seçmeliyim?

Aciliyet ve hacme bakın. Hava numune, ilk parti, sezon yakalama ve yüksek değerli küçük hacimli üründe mantıklı ama kilogram maliyeti denizin katları. Düzenli hacimde deniz standarttır; konteyneri dolduramıyorsanız LCL ile başlayıp hacim büyüdükçe FCL'e geçmek genelde en ucuz yoldur.

Malım kaç kez gümrükten geçiyor?

İki kez. Bir kez ABD'ye girerken, bir kez Meksika'ya geçerken. Türkiye menşeli mal her iki tarafta da tercihli tarifeden yararlanmaz, çünkü Türkiye'nin ne ABD ile bu kapsamda ne Meksika ile yürürlükte bir serbest ticaret anlaşması var. Bu, rota maliyetini hesaplarken en çok atlanan kalem.

ABD gümrük vergisini ödememem mümkün mü?

Mal ABD'de satılmayacaksa mevzuat iki araç sunuyor. Bonded depoda ithalat vergisi mal çıkana kadar ertelenir. Serbest bölgede mal henüz ABD'ye ithal edilmiş sayılmaz, dolayısıyla oradan Meksika'ya çıkan malda ABD vergisi hiç doğmayabilir. Hangisinin uygun olduğunu gümrük müşavirinle netleştir.

Laredo'da ne yapılıyor?

Teslim alma ve sayım, konsolidasyon, İspanyolca NOM etiketleme ve belge hazırlığı. Konsolidasyon en değerli kısmı: Meksika tarafındaki sabit maliyetler pedimento başına ödendiği için, birden fazla sevkiyatı tek ithalatta birleştirmek birim maliyeti belirgin şekilde düşürüyor.

translations.title: Meksika Ara Depo Hizmeti: Stoğu Sınırda Bekletmenin Gücü
translations.excerpt: Malı Meksika'ya sokar sokmaz vergisini ödüyor ve depolama saatini başlatıyorsun. Ara depo modeli bu iki saati de geciktiriyor.
translations.content:
Ara depo, malı Meksika'ya sokmadan sınırın ABD tarafında bekletmen ve talep geldikçe partiler hâlinde göndermen anlamına gelir. Böylece yüzde 16 IVA ve gümrük maliyetleri mal gerçekten gerektiğinde ödenir, Amazon veya yerel depo ücretleri gecikir ve satmayan ürüne sermaye bağlanmaz.

  • Ara depoda mal henüz Meksika'ya ithal edilmediği için ithalat vergileri o aşamada doğmaz.
  • İthalatta yüzde 16 IVA girişte ödenir ve akredite edilene kadar nakit bağlar (SAT).
  • Amazon Meksika depolama ücreti dm3 başına hesaplanır ve Ekim-Aralık arasında yükselir (Amazon México).
  • İyi belgelenmiş bir sevkiyat Laredo'dan Monterrey'e 1-2 iş gününde ulaşır (operasyon verisi).
  • Kısa reposition süresi, Meksika içinde tutulan stoğun küçük kalmasını mümkün kılar.

Ara depo modeli nasıl çalışır?

Mal sınırın ABD tarafındaki depoda bekler, Meksika'ya sadece satacağın kadarı gider. Böylece ithalat vergisi ve yerel depolama ücreti, mal gerçekten satışa hazır olduğunda başlar; öncesinde değil.

Ara depo, adı sade olduğu için hafife alınan ama nakit akışını doğrudan değiştiren bir model. Klasik yaklaşımda tedarikçiden gelen mal tek seferde Meksika'ya ithal edilir ve orada beklemeye başlar. O anda üç saat aynı anda çalışmaya başlar: gümrük vergisi ve yüzde 16 IVA ödenmiştir yani paran çıkmıştır, Meksika'daki depolama ücreti işlemeye başlamıştır, ve satmayan ürün için ayırdığın sermaye kilitlenmiştir. Ara depo modelinde bu sıralama değişir. Mal sınırın ABD tarafındaki depoya gelir ve orada bekler. Meksika'ya sadece önümüzdeki birkaç haftada satacağını tahmin ettiğin miktar geçer. Kalan stok, henüz Meksika'ya ithal edilmediği için o aşamada ithalat vergisi doğurmaz, Meksika depolama tarifesine tabi olmaz ve istersen rotasını değiştirebilirsin. Talep beklediğinden hızlı gelirse bir sonraki partiyi gönderirsin; iyi belgelenmiş bir sevkiyat Laredo'dan Monterrey'e 1-2 iş gününde ulaştığı için bu esneklik teorik değil, gerçek. Talep gelmezse malı hiç sokmamış olursun. Modelin özü bu: kararı ertelemek değil, maliyeti kararın verildiği ana kaydırmak.

Kim için mantıklı, kim için değil?

Talebi belirsiz, ürün çeşidi çok, sezonluk veya yeni pazara giren satıcı için mantıklı. Tek ürünlü, talebi istikrarlı ve hacmi yüksek satıcı için gereksiz bir ara adım olabilir.

Her modelde olduğu gibi bunun da uymadığı durumlar var ve dürüst olmak gerekiyor. Ara depo şu durumlarda net kazandırır. Birincisi, Meksika'ya yeni giriyorsan: hangi ürünün gerçekten döndüğünü bilmediğin dönemde bütün stoğu ithal etmek, öğrenme maliyetini gereksiz büyütür. İkincisi, ürün çeşidin çoksa: katalogunun büyük kısmı seyrek satan ürünlerden oluşuyorsa, hepsini içeri sokmak yerine dönenleri sokmak sermayeni korur. Üçüncüsü, sezonluk satıyorsan: sezon stoğunu erken ithal etmek hem depolama tarifesinin yükseldiği döneme denk gelir hem de sezon beklediğin gibi gitmezse elinde gümrüklenmiş ölü stok bırakır. Dördüncüsü, birden fazla kanala satıyorsan: aynı stoktan hem kendi sitene hem pazaryerine besleme yapmak, malı tek bir platformun deposuna kilitlemekten esnektir. Buna karşılık ara depo şu durumda gereksiz bir adım olabilir: tek veya az sayıda ürün satıyorsan, talebin istikrarlıysa ve hacmin yüksekse. O zaman malı doğrudan Meksika'ya sokup orada tutmak daha az elleçleme ve daha az koordinasyon demektir; ara depo katmanı sana esneklik satar ama senin esnekliğe ihtiyacın yoktur. Karar kriteri basit: talebini ne kadar iyi tahmin edebiliyorsan ara depoya o kadar az ihtiyacın var.

Nasıl kurarsın?

Ürünleri dönme hızına göre ayır, Meksika'da kaç haftalık stok tutacağına karar ver, yeniden sipariş noktası belirle ve etiketlemeyi sınırda hallet. Sonra ölç: hangi ürün ara depoda kalmalı, hangisi içeri girmeli.

Kurulum karmaşık değil ama sırayla yapılırsa çalışıyor. Önce ürünlerini son aylardaki satışa göre sırala ve dönme hızına göre ikiye ayır: düzenli satanlar ve seyrek satanlar. Düzenli satanlar Meksika içinde bulunmalı, seyrek satanlar ara depoda beklemeli. İkincisi, Meksika'da kaç haftalık stok tutacağına karar ver. Reposition kısa olduğu için bu sayı küçük olabilir; aylarca stok tutmak, ara deponun sağladığı avantajı geri verir. Üçüncüsü, her ürün için bir yeniden sipariş noktası belirle: stok o seviyenin altına düştüğünde bir sonraki parti otomatik tetiklensin, kimsenin hatırlamasına kalmasın. Dördüncüsü, etiketlemeyi ara depoda hallet. İspanyolca NOM etiketi Meksika'ya girişte gerekiyor, ve bunu sınırdaki depoda yapmak Meksika'da parça başına etiketlemekten ucuz. Beşincisi ölç: hangi ürünün ara depoda ne kadar beklediğini ve içeri girdikten sonra ne kadar hızlı satıldığını takip et. Bu veri, zamanla hangi ürünün doğrudan içeri girmesi gerektiğini sana söyler ve modeli kendi kendine ayarlar. BringGo Ship'in Laredo deposu ara depo işlevini, Monterrey deposu ise Meksika içi stok ve teslimatı karşılıyor, yani iki katman da tek zincirde duruyor.

  • Reposition: Reposition, sınırdaki depodan Meksika içindeki depoya yapılan stok tamamlama sevkiyatıdır.
  • Yeniden sipariş noktası: Yeniden sipariş noktası, stok o seviyeye düştüğünde bir sonraki partiyi otomatik tetikleyen eşiktir.

Sık sorulan sorular

Ara depo modeli nasıl çalışır?

Mal sınırın ABD tarafındaki depoda bekler, Meksika'ya sadece önümüzdeki birkaç haftada satacağın miktar geçer. Kalan stok henüz ithal edilmediği için o aşamada ithalat vergisi doğurmaz ve Meksika depolama tarifesine tabi olmaz. Talep geldikçe yeni parti gönderirsin.

Ara depo vergiyi tamamen ortadan kaldırır mı?

Hayır, erteler. Mal Meksika'ya girdiğinde gümrük vergisi ve yüzde 16 IVA doğar. Ara deponun sağladığı şey, bu maliyetin tüm stok için peşin değil, sadece gerçekten içeri giren parti için ödenmesi. Fark vergi oranında değil, nakit akışının zamanlamasında.

Kimler için mantıklı değil?

Tek veya az sayıda ürün satan, talebi istikrarlı ve hacmi yüksek satıcı için gereksiz bir ara adım olabilir. O durumda malı doğrudan Meksika'ya sokup orada tutmak daha az elleçleme demektir. Ara depo esneklik satar; esnekliğe ihtiyacın yoksa maliyetini boşuna ödersin.

Meksika'da ne kadar stok tutmalıyım?

Az. Reposition kısa olduğu için birkaç haftalık satış genelde yeterli. Aylarca stok tutmak ara deponun sağladığı avantajı geri verir. İyi belgelenmiş bir sevkiyat Laredo'dan Monterrey'e 1-2 iş gününde ulaştığı için sık ve küçük partiler çalışır.

Etiketleme nerede yapılmalı?

Ara depoda, yani mal Meksika'ya girmeden önce. İspanyolca NOM etiketi girişte gerekiyor ve sınırdaki depoda toplu yapmak, Meksika'da parça başına etiketlemekten belirgin şekilde ucuz. Ayrıca etiket eksikliği yüzünden gümrükte beklemeyi de önler.

translations.title: Binational Fulfillment: Serving US And Mexico From One Inventory Pool
translations.excerpt: Customs makes a single shared inventory pool impossible. What is possible is one forecast, one buying decision and one operator, with the border crossed on purpose rather than per order.
translations.content:
You cannot hold one legal inventory pool that serves both countries, because goods must be imported before they can be sold in Mexico. What you can do is run one planning system across two stocking points: a US warehouse that serves US customers and consolidates, and a Mexican warehouse that serves Mexican customers, replenished from the first in one to two business days.

  • Goods must be formally imported before they can be sold to Mexican customers, so a single legally shared pool is not possible.
  • A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days (operational data).
  • Short replenishment means the Mexican stocking point can hold weeks of cover rather than months.
  • Import IVA of 16 percent is paid on entry, so the size of the Mexican pool directly affects working capital (SAT).
  • Returns follow the same logic: each country needs a domestic return point or every return becomes an export.

How can I serve US and Mexican customers from one inventory?

Not literally, and it is worth being precise. Goods must be imported before they can be sold in Mexico, so you will always have two legal stocks. What you can unify is the planning: one forecast, one purchasing decision, one operator, two stocking points.

The phrase binational fulfillment gets used loosely, so it is worth separating what is possible from what is not. What is not possible is a single legal inventory that both markets draw from. Goods sold to a Mexican customer must have been imported into Mexico first, with an importer of record and a pedimento, and until that happens they are not sellable there. No warehouse arrangement changes that. What is entirely possible, and what the term should mean, is running one system across two stocking points. You forecast demand for both markets together, you buy once, and you decide deliberately how much of that purchase crosses the border and when. On the US side, a warehouse near the border serves US customers directly and acts as the consolidation point for everything heading south. On the Mexican side, a warehouse holds sellable stock and ships domestically. The link between them is short: a well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days. That short link is what makes the model work, because it means the Mexican stocking point does not need to be large. You are covering a replenishment window measured in days, not hedging against a supply line measured in weeks. The result is that you carry roughly the inventory of a single market while serving two.

Where the money is won and lost

Won by keeping the Mexican pool small and crossing on a reorder point. Lost by importing too much too early, which pays IVA and duty on stock that has not sold and leaves you with cleared inventory you cannot easily move back.

The economics of this model sit almost entirely in one decision: how much crosses, and when. Every unit you import into Mexico triggers costs at the moment it crosses. Import IVA of 16 percent is paid on entry, and although it is creditable, the cash leaves your business immediately. Duty depends on origin. Once cleared, the goods are inside Mexico, and moving them back is not a simple reversal, it is an export with its own process. So over importing is not a neutral mistake that resolves itself; it converts working capital into stock that is expensive to unwind. The discipline that prevents this is a reorder point per product rather than a shipping schedule. Instead of sending a big load monthly, you set a stock level per product that triggers the next consolidation, so what crosses is a response to demand that already happened rather than a forecast of demand that might. Because the crossing takes one to two business days, this works in practice and not just on paper. The second place money is won is consolidation. Fixed customs costs are paid per pedimento, not per pallet, so crossing more often in tiny loads is expensive. The balance most operations settle on is frequent enough to keep Mexican stock small, batched enough that each crossing carries meaningful volume. Finding that rhythm is worth more than negotiating freight rates.

Setting it up, including the part people forget

Split your catalogue by rotation, set reorder points, label before crossing, and design returns for both countries from the start. Returns are the piece that gets forgotten and the one that quietly undoes the savings.

Four decisions define the setup. First, split the catalogue. Your fastest moving products justify stock on both sides; the long tail does not, and should sit in the US pool and cross only when ordered or when it starts moving. Second, set reorder points per product rather than a calendar. Third, label before crossing. Goods entering Mexico need Spanish NOM labelling, and applying it at the US warehouse while cartons are open costs a fraction of relabelling per unit in Mexico. Fourth, and this is the one people leave until it hurts, design returns for both countries at the same time you design outbound. A US customer returns to a US address; a Mexican customer expects to return to a Mexican address. If the Mexican side has no local return point, every Mexican return becomes an export with its own paperwork and cost, and that cost lands on exactly the orders that were already unprofitable. Handled properly, returns actually strengthen the model: a unit returned in good condition in Mexico goes straight back into Mexican sellable stock without crossing anything, and only the small minority worth recovering travels north, consolidated. Set up this way, binational fulfillment stops being a slogan and becomes what it should be: one plan, two stocking points, and a border you cross on purpose rather than once per order. BringGo Ship runs warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey, which is what puts both stocking points and the crossing between them in a single chain.

Definitions

  • Stocking point: A stocking point is a warehouse holding sellable inventory for one market, as opposed to a legal inventory pool shared across borders.
  • Reorder point: A reorder point is the stock level that triggers the next cross-border replenishment automatically.
  • Long tail: The long tail is the majority of products that sell rarely and rarely justify holding stock on both sides of the border.

Frequently asked questions

Can one inventory pool really serve both the US and Mexico?

Not legally. Goods must be imported into Mexico with an importer of record and a pedimento before they can be sold there, so you will always have two legal stocks. What can be unified is the planning: one forecast, one purchasing decision, one operator, and two stocking points linked by a short crossing.

How much stock should I hold in Mexico?

Enough to cover the replenishment window, which is short. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days, so weeks of cover rather than months is usually right. Holding more converts working capital into cleared stock that is expensive to move back if demand does not appear.

What happens if I import too much into Mexico?

You pay import IVA of 16 percent and any duty on entry, and the cash leaves immediately even though the IVA is creditable. Once cleared, moving goods back is an export with its own process, not a simple reversal. Over importing is the most common and most expensive mistake in this model.

Should I cross more often or in bigger loads?

Both pull against each other. Fixed customs costs are paid per pedimento rather than per pallet, so many tiny crossings are expensive. But large infrequent crossings force you to hold more Mexican stock. Most operations settle on frequent enough to keep the Mexican pool small, batched enough that each crossing carries real volume.

What do people forget when setting this up?

Returns. A US customer returns to a US address and a Mexican customer expects a Mexican one. Without a local return point in Mexico, every Mexican return becomes an export with its own cost, landing on orders that were already thin. Designing returns alongside outbound is what protects the savings.

translations.title: Inventario Binacional: Atiende EE.UU. Y México Desde Un Solo Stock
translations.excerpt: Si ya vendes en México y quieres alcanzar al cliente estadounidense, el problema no es el transporte. Es dónde vive tu inventario y quién importa del otro lado.
translations.content:
No existe un solo inventario legal que sirva a los dos países, porque la mercancía debe importarse antes de venderse en cada mercado. Lo que sí funciona es un solo plan con dos puntos de stock: tu bodega en México para el cliente nacional y una bodega en la frontera estadounidense para atender al cliente de EE.UU. como envío doméstico.

  • La mercancía debe estar importada en cada país antes de poder venderse ahí, así que siempre habrá dos stocks legales.
  • Un camión bien documentado cubre el tramo Monterrey a Laredo en uno o dos días hábiles (dato operativo).
  • Para vender a un cliente en EE.UU. sin fricción, el producto debe estar del lado estadounidense antes de la venta.
  • Las devoluciones desde EE.UU. requieren una dirección de retorno estadounidense o el costo se dispara.
  • Los costos fijos aduanales se pagan por pedimento, así que consolidar reduce el costo por unidad en ambos sentidos.

¿Puedo atender ambos países con un solo inventario?

Con un solo inventario legal no, porque cada país exige importación previa. Con un solo plan sí: compras una vez, decides cuánto vive en México y cuánto cruza al norte, y cada mercado recibe envíos domésticos.

Vale la pena ser preciso con el término, porque inventario binacional suena a algo que no existe. No hay una figura que permita que una misma mercancía esté simultáneamente disponible para venta en México y en Estados Unidos: cada país exige que el producto haya sido importado antes de venderse ahí. Lo que sí existe, y es lo que funciona en la práctica, es una operación con un solo plan y dos puntos de stock. Si ya vendes en México, tu punto de stock nacional ya está resuelto. Lo que falta para alcanzar al comprador estadounidense es tener producto del lado norte antes de la venta. Esto importa más de lo que parece, porque el cliente estadounidense compara tu tiempo de entrega con el de un vendedor local. Si tu producto sale de México cada vez que alguien compra, tu envío es internacional: más lento, más caro y con formalidades que el comprador no espera. Si tu producto ya está en una bodega estadounidense, tu envío es doméstico y compites en igualdad. El tramo entre ambos puntos es corto: un camión bien documentado cubre Monterrey a Laredo en uno o dos días hábiles, lo cual permite que el stock del norte sea pequeño y se reponga seguido en lugar de acumularse.

Lo que cambia al vender hacia el norte

Cambian tres cosas: alguien tiene que importar del lado estadounidense, las devoluciones necesitan dirección en EE.UU., y el arancel depende del origen de tu mercancía, no de dónde esté tu empresa.

Exportar hacia el norte no es simplemente el mismo flujo al revés, y conviene ver las tres diferencias antes de montarlo. La primera es quién importa. Igual que en México se necesita un importador registrado, del lado estadounidense la entrada formal tiene su propio responsable y sus propias formalidades. Si vendes a consumidores, la mercancía debe estar ya nacionalizada allá, porque no puedes dejar que cada comprador resuelva su propia importación. La segunda es la devolución. El comprador estadounidense espera devolver a una dirección local, y si tu única dirección de retorno está en México, cada devolución se convierte en un envío internacional cuyo costo suele superar el valor del producto. Una dirección de retorno en Estados Unidos deja de ser un lujo y pasa a ser parte del costo de vender allá. La tercera, y la que más sorprende, es el arancel. El trato arancelario depende del origen de la mercancía, no de dónde esté constituida tu empresa. Un producto fabricado en México que califica bajo el T-MEC entra a Estados Unidos con trato preferencial siempre que exista certificado de origen. Un producto que compraste importado de Asia y solo revendes desde México no adquiere origen mexicano por haber pasado por aquí. Esa distinción decide el margen de la operación y conviene resolverla antes de fijar precios.

Cómo se organiza sin duplicar capital

Separa el catálogo por rotación, deja el grueso en México y manda al norte solo lo que se vende allá, con punto de reorden. Consolida los cruces y resuelve la devolución en cada país desde el principio.

El objetivo es atender dos mercados sin financiar dos inventarios completos, y se logra con cuatro decisiones. Primero, separa el catálogo por rotación en cada mercado, no en general: lo que se vende bien en México no necesariamente se vende bien allá. Solo las referencias con demanda comprobada del lado norte justifican stock ahí; el resto se queda en México. Segundo, define un punto de reorden por producto para el stock del norte, de modo que la reposición se dispare por el nivel de inventario y no por el calendario. Como el tramo es de uno a dos días hábiles, esto permite mantener el stock estadounidense pequeño. Tercero, consolida los cruces. Los costos fijos aduanales se pagan por pedimento y no por tarima, así que cruzar seguido en cargas mínimas encarece; el equilibrio suele estar en cruzar con la frecuencia suficiente para no quedarte sin stock, pero agrupando volumen real en cada cruce. Cuarto, resuelve la devolución en ambos lados desde el inicio, no cuando llegue la primera. Cada mercado necesita su punto de retorno local; sin eso, las devoluciones cruzan la frontera de una en una y se comen el margen justo de los pedidos que ya venían apretados. Montado así, no duplicas capital: financias aproximadamente el inventario de un mercado y atiendes dos. BringGo Ship opera bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey, de modo que ambos puntos de stock y el cruce entre ellos quedan en una sola cadena.

Definiciones

  • Punto de stock: Un punto de stock es una bodega que guarda inventario ya nacionalizado y listo para venderse en ese mercado.
  • Punto de reorden: El punto de reorden es el nivel de inventario que dispara automáticamente la siguiente reposición hacia el otro lado.
  • Origen de la mercancía: El origen es dónde se produjo el bien, y determina el trato arancelario con independencia de dónde esté constituida tu empresa.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Puedo vender en EE.UU. y México con un solo inventario?

Con un solo inventario legal no, porque cada país exige que la mercancía esté importada antes de venderse ahí. Lo que sí se puede es un solo plan con dos puntos de stock: tu bodega mexicana para el cliente nacional y una bodega del lado estadounidense para atender allá como envío doméstico.

¿Por qué necesito stock del lado estadounidense?

Porque el comprador allá compara tu tiempo de entrega con el de un vendedor local. Si el producto sale de México en cada venta, tu envío es internacional: más lento, más caro y con formalidades que el cliente no espera. Con stock allá, tu envío es doméstico y compites en igualdad.

¿Mi producto entra a EE.UU. sin arancel por ser mexicano?

Depende del origen de la mercancía, no de dónde esté tu empresa. Un producto fabricado en México que califica bajo el T-MEC entra con trato preferencial si existe certificado de origen. Un producto que importaste de Asia y solo revendes desde México no adquiere origen mexicano por haber pasado por aquí.

¿Qué pasa con las devoluciones desde EE.UU.?

El comprador espera devolver a una dirección local. Si tu única dirección de retorno está en México, cada devolución se vuelve un envío internacional cuyo costo suele superar el valor del producto. Una dirección de retorno en Estados Unidos es parte del costo de vender allá, no un extra opcional.

¿Cómo evito duplicar mi inversión en inventario?

Manda al norte solo las referencias con demanda comprobada allá, define un punto de reorden por producto y consolida los cruces. Como el tramo Monterrey a Laredo es de uno o dos días hábiles, el stock del lado norte puede ser pequeño y reponerse seguido en lugar de acumularse.

translations.title: US Return Address For Mexican Sellers: Handling Northbound Returns
translations.excerpt: A Mexican seller reaching US customers hits the same wall in reverse: without a US return address, every return becomes an export and the cost usually exceeds the product.
translations.content:
A Mexican seller selling to US customers needs a return address inside the United States. Without one, each return is an international shipment whose cost usually exceeds the value of the product. With one, the return is a domestic parcel, the unit can be inspected and restocked in the US, and only the small share worth recovering travels south consolidated.

  • US buyers expect a domestic return address and compare your policy against local sellers.
  • Without a US address, each return becomes an international shipment with its own formalities and cost.
  • Returned units in resellable condition can go straight back into US sellable stock rather than crossing the border twice.
  • Only the minority of units genuinely worth recovering should travel south, and they should travel consolidated.
  • A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days (operational data).

How do Mexican sellers handle returns from US customers?

By having an address inside the United States that receives them. It does not need to be your own facility. What matters is that the buyer ships domestically and that someone inspects the unit before deciding what happens to it.

A Mexican company selling into the United States runs into the mirror image of the problem US sellers face going south, and it is worth stating plainly because the solution is the same shape. Your US customer expects to return the way they return to any local store: print a label, drop the parcel, get refunded. If your only return address is in Mexico, that is not what happens. The parcel becomes an international shipment, it needs documentation, it moves at international speed, and the cost of moving one item is wildly out of proportion to the item itself. In most consumer categories the return shipping alone exceeds the product value, which pushes sellers into two bad habits: refusing returns, which damages the listing and invites disputes, or refunding without recovering the goods, which means eating the full cost of every return. The third option is an address inside the United States. It does not have to be a facility you own; a logistics partner operating there provides the same thing. The customer ships domestically, which is fast and cheap for them, the parcel arrives in days rather than weeks, and you get the thing that actually matters: possession of the unit and the ability to inspect it before deciding what it is worth. That single change turns returns from a fixed loss into a recovery process.

What to do with the unit once it arrives

Log it against the order, grade it, then send it down one of three paths: back into US sellable stock, into a secondary channel, or disposal. Sending it back to Mexico should be the exception, and when it happens it should be consolidated.

A return address is just a mailbox until there is a process behind it, and the process is short. Step one is intake: record what arrived and match it to an order, because an unmatched return is a refund dispute waiting to happen. Step two is inspection and grading, sorting units honestly into condition tiers rather than treating them as one pile. From there, three paths. Units in resellable condition go straight back into your US inventory and sell again to the next US customer. This is the path that makes the whole model pay, because the unit becomes revenue without crossing any border in either direction. Units with damaged packaging or light wear go to a secondary channel, which depending on your category might be a discounted listing, a refurbished offer or a bundle. Units that are genuinely unsellable go to disposal, and it is worth being decisive here rather than paying to store things that will never sell. Only after this sorting does sending anything to Mexico make sense. Usually the answer is that a minority of units justify it, and when they do they should travel together in one consolidated shipment rather than one at a time. A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days, so batching costs you very little time and saves a great deal of money.

Setting it up, and the second thing it buys you

Decide who receives, publish a clear English return policy, write down grading rules, and set a consolidation rhythm. The same US facility that handles returns also serves as the forward stocking point that makes your US delivery times competitive.

Four decisions get this running. First, who receives the returns. Very few Mexican sellers need their own US facility for this, because returns volume is a fraction of outbound volume and a lease plus staff rarely pays for itself; most use a partner already operating there. Second, what the customer sees: a return policy in English, easy to find, specific about the window, the condition expected and how the refund is issued. Vague policies generate support tickets and chargebacks rather than clean returns. Third, the grading rulebook, written before the first return arrives so the decision does not depend on who opens the box. Fourth, the consolidation rhythm, meaning how often the small number of recoverable units travel south. Then there is a second benefit that often matters more than the returns themselves. The same US facility that receives returns can hold forward stock for US orders. Once you have inventory sitting in the United States, your US delivery times stop being international and start being domestic, which is the single biggest factor in whether a US buyer chooses you over a local seller. In other words, the infrastructure you build to stop losing money on returns is the same infrastructure that lets you compete properly in that market. Definitions

  • Northbound return: A northbound return is a product sent back by a US customer to a seller based in Mexico.
  • Grading: Grading is sorting returned units by condition so each follows the right path: restock, secondary channel or disposal.
  • Forward stock: Forward stock is inventory held inside the destination market so orders ship domestically rather than internationally.

Frequently asked questions

Do Mexican sellers need a US return address?

In practice yes, if you sell to US consumers. Buyers expect to return the way they do to any local store. Without a US address each return is an international shipment whose cost usually exceeds the product value, which pushes sellers into refusing returns or refunding without recovering the goods.

Does the return address have to be my own facility?

No. Returns volume is normally a fraction of outbound volume, so a lease and staff rarely pay for themselves. Most Mexican sellers use a logistics partner already operating in the United States. What matters is that the buyer ships domestically and that someone inspects the unit before deciding what it is worth.

What happens to returned units that are still good?

They go straight back into your US sellable stock and sell again to the next US customer. This is the path that makes the model pay, because the unit becomes revenue without crossing any border in either direction. Sending it home to Mexico would mean paying to move it twice for no gain.

Should I ship returns back to Mexico?

Only the minority where recovered value clearly justifies it, and then consolidated rather than one at a time. A well documented truck covers Monterrey to Laredo in one to two business days, so batching costs very little time and saves a great deal of money compared with individual shipments.

Is there any benefit beyond cheaper returns?

Yes, and it is often bigger. The same US facility can hold forward stock for US orders. Once inventory sits in the United States your delivery times stop being international and become domestic, which is the main factor in whether a US buyer chooses you over a local seller.

translations.title: Restricción Horaria Para Tráileres En Monterrey: Cómo Planear Entregas
translations.excerpt: Tu carga puede llegar a tiempo a Monterrey y aun así no poder entregarse. La restricción de circulación es municipal y cambia, y planear sin conocerla cuesta un día.
translations.content:
En la zona metropolitana de Monterrey la circulación de vehículos de carga pesada está regulada a nivel municipal, con horarios y rutas que varían entre municipios y que se actualizan. La consecuencia práctica es que una carga puede llegar a tiempo y aun así no poder entregarse hasta la siguiente ventana permitida, así que la entrega se programa contra el horario local y no solo contra el tránsito.

  • La circulación de carga pesada en la zona metro de Monterrey se regula por municipio, no por una sola norma estatal uniforme.
  • Los horarios y rutas permitidas cambian, por lo que deben confirmarse con el transportista antes de programar la entrega.
  • Una carga puede llegar dentro del tiempo de tránsito y aun así esperar a la siguiente ventana permitida para entregar.
  • Un camión bien documentado cubre Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles (dato operativo).
  • Entregar en zonas industriales suele ser más flexible que entregar en zonas urbanas o comerciales densas.

¿A qué horas pueden circular tráileres en Monterrey?

Depende del municipio. La zona metropolitana está formada por varios municipios y cada uno regula la circulación de carga pesada con sus propios horarios y rutas. Por eso no existe una sola respuesta válida para toda el área y hay que confirmarla antes de programar.

Aquí conviene ser honesto en lugar de dar una cifra que suene precisa. La zona metropolitana de Monterrey no es un solo municipio: incluye Monterrey, San Pedro Garza García, Guadalupe, San Nicolás, Apodaca, Escobedo, Santa Catarina y otros, y la circulación de vehículos de carga pesada se regula a nivel municipal. Cada municipio define sus propias restricciones de horario y sus rutas permitidas, y esas disposiciones se actualizan. Publicar aquí un horario fijo sería cómodo pero te induciría al error, porque el horario que aplica a tu entrega depende de en qué municipio está la dirección de destino y de la norma vigente ese mes. Lo que sí podemos decir con seguridad es qué lógica siguen estas restricciones, porque es consistente. Buscan sacar los vehículos pesados de las vías urbanas en las horas de mayor congestión, proteger ciertas zonas residenciales, comerciales y escolares, y canalizar la carga por corredores diseñados para soportarla. De ahí se derivan tres implicaciones prácticas: las ventanas de entrega tienden a abrirse fuera de las horas pico, las zonas industriales suelen ser más flexibles que las urbanas densas, y el tipo de vehículo importa, porque lo que se restringe casi siempre son las unidades de mayor tamaño y peso.

Por qué esto cambia tu planeación, no solo tu ruta

Porque el tiempo de tránsito y la hora de entrega son cosas distintas. Un camión puede llegar en el plazo previsto y aun así esperar a la siguiente ventana permitida, y esa espera se convierte en un día perdido si nadie la contempló.

El error más común no es incumplir la norma, es planear como si no existiera. Un camión bien documentado cubre Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles, y esa cifra es real, pero describe el tránsito, no la entrega. Si la unidad llega a la zona metropolitana fuera de la ventana permitida para su tipo de vehículo en ese municipio, no entrega: espera. Y una espera de unas horas suele convertirse en un día completo, porque el destinatario también tiene horario de recepción. Cuando ese día no estaba contemplado, aparece como retraso del transportista aunque nadie haya hecho nada mal. La segunda consecuencia es sobre el tipo de unidad. Si tu destino final está en una zona con restricción fuerte, mover la carga hasta ahí en un tráiler completo puede ser inviable, y la solución operativa es transferir a una unidad más pequeña en un punto intermedio. Eso es una decisión de diseño de red, no una improvisación del día de la entrega: implica un punto donde hacer la transferencia y un costo adicional que debe estar en la cotización desde el inicio. La tercera consecuencia es sobre las citas. En destinos con ventana estrecha, la cita de entrega deja de ser un trámite y pasa a ser el eje de la programación: primero se consigue la cita, después se planea el cruce.

Qué preguntar antes de programar

Pregunta el municipio del destino, si aplica restricción a tu tipo de unidad, cuál es la ventana permitida hoy, si el destino tiene horario de recepción propio y si hará falta transferir a una unidad menor. Cinco preguntas antes de cotizar, no después.

La forma de no perder días es convertir esto en cinco preguntas que se hacen antes de cerrar la operación. Primera: ¿en qué municipio está exactamente la dirección de entrega? No basta con decir Monterrey, porque la zona metropolitana abarca varios municipios con reglas distintas. Segunda: ¿aplica restricción de circulación al tipo de unidad que va a llevar mi carga? Lo que se restringe suele ser el tamaño y el peso, así que la respuesta cambia según si va en tráiler completo o en unidad menor. Tercera: ¿cuál es la ventana permitida vigente para ese municipio? Vigente es la palabra clave, porque estas disposiciones se actualizan y una referencia del año pasado puede estar desfasada; tu transportista local es quien tiene el dato actual. Cuarta: ¿el destino tiene su propio horario de recepción y requiere cita? En muchos casos esa ventana es más estrecha que la municipal y termina siendo la restricción que manda. Quinta: ¿va a hacer falta transferir a una unidad más pequeña, y ese costo está en la cotización? Si la respuesta es sí y no estaba cotizado, aparecerá como cargo extra al final. Un operador que trabaja el corredor a diario responde estas cinco sin dudar, y esa es una buena forma de distinguir a quien conoce la ciudad de quien solo mueve carga hasta la frontera. BringGo Ship opera bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey, de modo que el cruce, la entrega local y la programación se planean juntos.

Definiciones

  • Ventana de entrega: La ventana de entrega es el rango horario en el que un vehículo de carga puede circular y entregar en un municipio determinado.
  • Transferencia a unidad menor: Es pasar la carga de un tráiler a un vehículo más pequeño en un punto intermedio para poder entrar a zonas con restricción.
  • Zona metropolitana de Monterrey: Es el conjunto de municipios alrededor de Monterrey, cada uno con su propia regulación de circulación de carga.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿A qué horas pueden circular tráileres en Monterrey?

Depende del municipio. La zona metropolitana incluye varios municipios y cada uno regula la circulación de carga pesada con sus propios horarios y rutas, que además se actualizan. No existe una sola respuesta válida para toda el área, así que hay que confirmarla con el transportista antes de programar.

¿Por qué mi carga llegó a tiempo y no se entregó?

Porque el tiempo de tránsito y la hora de entrega son cosas distintas. Si la unidad llega fuera de la ventana permitida para su tipo de vehículo en ese municipio, espera a la siguiente. Una espera de horas suele convertirse en un día completo, porque el destinatario también tiene horario de recepción.

¿Qué lógica siguen estas restricciones?

Sacar los vehículos pesados de las vías urbanas en horas de mayor congestión, proteger zonas residenciales, comerciales y escolares, y canalizar la carga por corredores diseñados para soportarla. Por eso las zonas industriales suelen ser más flexibles que las zonas urbanas densas.

¿Voy a necesitar cambiar a un camión más pequeño?

Es posible si el destino está en una zona con restricción fuerte. La solución operativa es transferir la carga a una unidad menor en un punto intermedio. Eso implica un punto de transferencia y un costo adicional, y debe estar en la cotización desde el inicio para que no aparezca como cargo extra al final.

¿Qué debo preguntar antes de programar una entrega?

El municipio exacto del destino, si aplica restricción a tu tipo de unidad, cuál es la ventana permitida vigente, si el destinatario tiene su propio horario de recepción y si hará falta transferir a una unidad menor con su costo. Un operador que trabaja el corredor a diario responde las cinco sin dudar.

translations.title: What Is A Pedimento? Mexico's Customs Declaration Explained
translations.excerpt: If you ship to Mexico you will hear this word constantly. It is not paperwork you can skip or file yourself, and understanding it explains most of how Mexican customs works.
translations.content:
A pedimento is the official Mexican customs declaration that legalises the import or export of goods. It records what the goods are, their tariff classification, their customs value, their origin and the duties and taxes paid. Only a licensed Mexican customs broker can file it, and without it goods cannot legally enter Mexico as a commercial import.

  • The pedimento is the document that legalises a commercial import or export in Mexico (SAT).
  • Only a licensed Mexican customs broker, an agente aduanal with a patente, can file it (SAT).
  • It records the tariff classification, customs value, origin, and the duties and taxes paid.
  • Mexican tariff codes are ten digits: eight for the fracción arancelaria plus two for the NICO (RGCE 2026).
  • Correcting a wrongly declared field afterwards is a formal rectification with its own cost and time.

What is a pedimento?

It is Mexico's official customs declaration. It states what the goods are, how they are classified, what they are worth, where they came from and what was paid. Without it, a commercial import has not legally happened.

If you ship anything commercially into Mexico you will hear this word in every conversation, so it is worth understanding properly rather than treating it as generic paperwork. A pedimento is the formal customs declaration filed with the Mexican authorities to legalise the entry or exit of goods. It is not a shipping document like a bill of lading, and it is not an invoice. It is the legal act of declaring, and the moment it is filed and cleared, the goods have entered Mexico lawfully and can circulate and be sold there. Before that moment they cannot, no matter where they physically are. The document records a specific set of facts: what the goods are, the tariff classification they fall under, the customs value on which taxes are calculated, the country of origin, the regime under which they enter, who the importer of record is, and the duties and taxes paid. Because it is a legal declaration rather than a description, accuracy matters in a way that shipping paperwork does not. The person whose name is on it is asserting that these facts are true, and the authority can verify them. This is also why the pedimento is the reference document for everything afterwards: if you need to prove what you imported, when, at what value and under what classification, the pedimento is the answer.

Who files it, and what is on it

Only a licensed Mexican customs broker can file a pedimento. It carries the tariff code, customs value, origin, regime, importer details and the taxes paid, and each of those fields carries consequences if declared wrongly.

The filing itself is restricted. Only a licensed Mexican customs broker, known as an agente aduanal and holding a patente, can present a pedimento. This is not a formality you can handle yourself, and your freight carrier cannot do it for you either. It is the single most common surprise for companies entering the Mexican market: you may organize everything else, but this step requires a licensed professional by law. On the content side, a few fields deserve attention because they drive both cost and risk. The tariff classification determines the duty rate and which non-tariff regulations apply to your product, and Mexican codes run to ten digits: the first eight are the fracción arancelaria and the last two are the NICO, a commercial identification number. As of 2026, an incorrect or missing NICO became explicitly sanctionable in its own right, not just the eight digit code. The customs value is the basis on which taxes are calculated and must be consistent with your commercial invoice. The origin field determines whether preferential treatment applies, which is why a USMCA certification of origin matters so much: with it, qualifying US goods enter duty free, without it they pay the general rate. And the regime states whether the goods are entering permanently, temporarily, or under a special program, which changes what obligations follow.

Why it matters to you in practice

Because most import problems are pedimento problems. Wrong classification, inconsistent value or missing origin documentation is what stops shipments, and fixing a filed declaration afterwards is a formal rectification with cost and delay attached.

Understanding the pedimento explains most of what goes wrong at the Mexican border, and almost none of it is about trucks. Shipments get held because a declared field does not match reality: the classification does not fit the product, the invoice value does not match the declaration, the description is too generic to identify what is inside, or the origin claim has no certification behind it. Each of these is a pedimento issue rather than a logistics issue, which is why the quality of your documentation predicts your transit time better than the distance does. There is also a cost consequence. Correcting a declared field after filing is a formal rectification with its own charge and its own delay, and if the discrepancy is significant it can escalate beyond a correction. Under Mexican rules, if the commercial description on the pedimento genuinely matches the physical goods, a wrong tariff classification is treated as an inexact data declaration with a bounded penalty rather than as something more serious, but if the description does not match, or if the wrong code sidesteps a permit or a standard, the position changes substantially. The practical takeaway is simple: the work that determines whether your import goes smoothly happens before the goods move, in getting the classification, the value, the description and the origin documentation right. BringGo Ship prepares that documentation as part of the shipment, so it is ready for the licensed broker rather than becoming a separate problem you have to solve.

The pedimento at a glance

FieldWhat it determinesRisk if wrong
Tariff classificationDuty rate and regulationsRectification, or worse if it evades a rule
NICO (last two digits)Commercial identificationSanctionable in its own right since 2026
Customs valueTax baseMust match the commercial invoice
OriginWhether preference appliesNo certification means general rate
RegimePermanent, temporary or specialChanges the obligations that follow
Who files itLicensed customs broker onlyCannot be filed by you or your carrier

The obligation is written into the Customs Law itself, and it is worth reading in the original because it defines both what a pedimento is and how it must be filed:

“Quienes introduzcan o extraigan mercancías del territorio nacional destinándolas a un régimen aduanero, están obligados a transmitir a las autoridades aduaneras, a través del sistema electrónico aduanero, en documento electrónico, un pedimento con información referente a las citadas mercancías.”

Ley Aduanera, Article 36 (Mexico)

Definitions

  • Pedimento: A pedimento is Mexico's official customs declaration that legalises the import or export of goods.
  • Agente aduanal: An agente aduanal is the licensed Mexican customs broker, holding a patente, who is the only party able to file a pedimento.
  • Fracción arancelaria: The fracción arancelaria is the first eight digits of the Mexican tariff code, followed by two NICO digits for a ten digit total.

Frequently asked questions

What is a pedimento in Mexican customs?

It is the official customs declaration that legalises the import or export of goods. It records what the goods are, their tariff classification, customs value, origin, the regime they enter under and the duties and taxes paid. Until it is filed and cleared, a commercial import has not legally happened.

Can I file a pedimento myself?

No. Only a licensed Mexican customs broker, an agente aduanal holding a patente, can present a pedimento. Your freight carrier cannot do it either. This is the most common surprise for companies entering Mexico: you can arrange everything else, but this step requires a licensed professional by law.

What does a pedimento contain?

The description of the goods, the tariff classification, the customs value on which taxes are calculated, the country of origin, the customs regime, the importer of record and the duties and taxes paid. Mexican tariff codes run to ten digits: eight for the fracción arancelaria plus two for the NICO.

What happens if something on the pedimento is wrong?

Correcting a declared field after filing is a formal rectification with its own cost and delay. If the commercial description genuinely matches the physical goods, a wrong classification is treated as inexact data with a bounded penalty. If the description does not match, or the wrong code sidesteps a permit or standard, the consequences are considerably more serious.

Why do shipments to Mexico get held?

Usually because of a pedimento issue rather than a transport issue. The classification does not fit the product, the invoice value does not match the declaration, the description is too generic, or an origin claim has no certification behind it. Documentation quality predicts transit time far better than distance does.

translations.title: US To Mexico Freight Forwarder: What They Do And What They Do Not
translations.excerpt: Freight forwarder, customs broker, 3PL: three different roles that get used interchangeably. Knowing which one you actually need is what stops your freight sitting at the border.
translations.content:
A freight forwarder arranges and coordinates transport but does not clear goods through customs. In Mexico only a licensed customs broker can file the pedimento. A cross-border 3PL combines both plus warehousing and delivery, which is why most shippers moving goods between the US and Mexico end up needing more than a forwarder alone.

  • A freight forwarder arranges transport and documentation but does not itself clear goods through customs.
  • In Mexico only a licensed customs broker, an agente aduanal with a patente, can file the pedimento (SAT).
  • A cross-border 3PL combines forwarding, clearance, warehousing and final delivery under one accountable party.
  • Trucking carries roughly 73 to 74 percent of US Mexico trade, so most freight in this lane moves by road (WorldCity, Census).
  • A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days (operational data).

What does a freight forwarder actually do?

Arranges transport. A forwarder books capacity, coordinates carriers, prepares transport documentation and tracks the shipment. What a forwarder does not do is clear your goods through Mexican customs, because that requires a separate license.

The term freight forwarder gets used as a catch all for anyone who moves goods internationally, which is why so many shippers end up with the wrong provider for their situation. A forwarder is an organiser of transport. They book capacity with carriers, coordinate the legs of a journey, prepare and manage transport documentation, consolidate shipments where that makes sense, and give you visibility over where your goods are. For a shipment moving from Asia to the United States, a competent forwarder may be all you need, because they handle the movement and a customs broker on the US side handles the entry. The US to Mexico lane works differently and this is where the confusion costs money. Mexico requires that the customs declaration, the pedimento, be filed by a licensed Mexican customs broker holding a patente. A freight forwarder, however capable, cannot do this unless they also hold that license or work with someone who does. So when a forwarder quotes you a rate to Mexico, the honest question to ask is what happens at the border: do they clear the goods themselves, do they hand off to a broker they work with, or do they hand off to you. Those three answers describe very different services, and the third one is where shipments sit while someone works out who is responsible.

Forwarder, customs broker or 3PL: which do you need?

A forwarder if you only need transport arranged and you already have clearance covered. A customs broker if you have transport handled and need the pedimento filed. A cross-border 3PL if you want one party accountable from pickup to final delivery, which is most shippers.

The three roles are complementary rather than competing, and picking correctly is a matter of what you already have covered. A freight forwarder is right when your constraint is capacity and coordination: you know how to clear goods in Mexico, you have a broker, and you need someone to organize the movement. A customs broker is right when your constraint is compliance: your transport is arranged, perhaps by your buyer or an existing carrier, and what you need is the entry filed correctly. Note that in Mexico this is not optional for commercial imports, so you will need a broker in some form regardless. A cross-border 3PL is right when your constraint is that you do not want to manage the border at all. This kind of operator combines the forwarder role, the customs broker role, warehousing on one or both sides, and final delivery, under a single accountable party. Most companies shipping regularly between the US and Mexico converge on this because of what the alternative looks like in practice: three providers, each responsible for their own leg, and a handoff at the border where a problem belongs to nobody. Since trucking carries roughly three quarters of US Mexico trade, most of this happens by road, where handoffs are physical: a trailer waits while the next party accepts responsibility for it.

What to ask before you choose

Ask who files the pedimento, whether they have warehouses on both sides, whether they can label and prepare goods before crossing, and whether you get one invoice and one contact. The answers separate a coordinator from an operator.

Four questions do most of the work in separating providers, and they can be asked in a single email. First, who files the pedimento? If they can name the licensed broker, you are talking to an operator who knows the lane. If the answer is vague, that can still work but ask how the handoff works and who is accountable if it goes wrong. If the answer is that you need to arrange it, you are buying transport only, and you should price the missing piece before comparing quotes. Second, do you have warehouses on both sides of the border? This determines whether they can consolidate before the crossing, which is where the customs cost per unit falls, and whether they can hold and deliver inside Mexico afterwards. Third, can you prepare goods before crossing? Spanish NOM labelling has to happen before goods are offered for sale in Mexico, and doing it at a border warehouse is far cheaper than relabelling per unit after arrival. Fourth, do I get one invoice and one point of contact? This sounds like a convenience question and it is really an accountability question: when responsibility is split across three companies, the gaps between them are where shipments stall. As for transit itself, that is rarely the differentiator. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days regardless of who booked it. What differs between providers is what happens in the hours around the border, not on the highway. BringGo Ship operates warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey on the same lane, which is the profile these four questions are designed to find.

Who does what on the US Mexico lane

RoleArranges transportFiles the pedimento
Freight forwarderYesNo, unless licensed or partnered
Mexican customs brokerNoYes, exclusively
Cross-border 3PLYesCoordinated with a licensed broker
Warehousing both sidesForwarder rarely3PL typically
Spanish NOM labellingRarely3PL at the border
Single accountable partyNo3PL, one invoice one contact

Definitions

  • Freight forwarder: A freight forwarder arranges and coordinates transport and documentation but does not itself clear goods through customs.
  • Customs broker: In Mexico a customs broker is the licensed professional who is the only party permitted to file the pedimento.
  • Cross-border 3PL: A cross-border 3PL combines forwarding, customs clearance, warehousing and delivery under a single accountable party.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a freight forwarder and a customs broker?

A freight forwarder arranges transport, books capacity, prepares transport documentation and tracks the shipment. A customs broker files the customs declaration. In Mexico only a licensed customs broker with a patente can file the pedimento, so a forwarder alone cannot clear your goods into the country.

Do I need a freight forwarder for shipping to Mexico?

Only if you need transport arranged and coordinated. If you already have carriers and a broker, you may not. What you cannot skip for a commercial import is the licensed Mexican customs broker, because the pedimento can only be filed by one. Most regular shippers use a cross-border 3PL that covers both roles.

Can a US freight forwarder clear my goods into Mexico?

Not by themselves. Mexican clearance requires a licensed Mexican customs broker. A US forwarder may work with one, which is a normal arrangement, but ask specifically how the handoff works and who is accountable if something goes wrong at the border. If they say you need to arrange clearance, you are buying transport only.

What should I ask a provider before choosing?

Who files the pedimento, whether they have warehouses on both sides of the border, whether they can apply Spanish NOM labelling before crossing, and whether you get one invoice and one point of contact. These four answers separate a transport coordinator from an operator who owns the border.

Does the choice affect how fast my freight arrives?

Less than people expect on the road, more than people expect at the border. A well documented truck reaches Monterrey from Laredo in one to two business days regardless of who booked it. What differs is what happens in the hours around the crossing, where incomplete documentation and unclear responsibility cause the delays.

translations.title: Envíos De Estados Unidos A México: Todas Las Opciones Explicadas
translations.excerpt: Enviar de Estados Unidos a México tiene tres caminos reales y la diferencia de costo entre ellos es enorme. La elección correcta depende del volumen, no del precio de lista.
translations.content:
Hay tres formas de enviar de Estados Unidos a México: mensajería paquete por paquete, carga consolidada que cruza en una sola importación, y camión completo. La mensajería sirve para envíos ocasionales, la consolidación baja el costo por unidad al repartir los gastos fijos del pedimento, y el camión completo aplica cuando el volumen llena una unidad.

  • El régimen simplificado de mensajería tiene un tope de 2,500 dólares por destinatario (RGCE 2026).
  • La mercancía de origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento de arancel bajo el T-MEC si hay certificado de origen (SAT, USTR).
  • El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana a nivel nacional (SAT).
  • Los costos fijos de una importación se pagan por pedimento, no por tarima, así que consolidar baja el costo por unidad.
  • Un camión bien documentado llega de Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles (dato operativo).

¿Cómo enviar productos de USA a México?

Por mensajería si son envíos ocasionales y pequeños, por carga consolidada si compras seguido a uno o varios proveedores, o en camión completo si llenas una unidad. La diferencia real entre ellas no es la velocidad, es cuántas veces pagas los costos fijos de aduana.

Las tres opciones existen para volúmenes distintos, y elegir mal es la razón más común por la que un importador nuevo termina con costos que no cuadran. La mensajería mueve paquete por paquete. Es rápida de arrancar, no exige montar nada, y bajo el régimen simplificado tiene un tope de 2,500 dólares por destinatario. Su debilidad aparece con la repetición: cada paquete pasa por su propio trámite, así que el costo por unidad se mantiene alto sin importar cuánto compres. La carga consolidada junta mercancía de uno o varios proveedores en una bodega del lado estadounidense y la cruza en una sola importación formal, con pedimento presentado por agente aduanal. Aquí está la palanca económica más importante de todo el proceso: los costos fijos de la importación, es decir el honorario del agente, la prevalidación y el derecho de trámite, se pagan por pedimento y no por tarima. Traer cuatro proveedores en un solo cruce reparte esos montos entre cuatro veces más mercancía. El camión completo aplica cuando tu volumen llena una unidad hacia un mismo destino, y entonces deja de tener sentido compartir espacio. La velocidad, curiosamente, no es lo que más cambia: un camión bien documentado llega de Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles en cualquiera de los esquemas.

Qué se paga en cada caso

IVA del 16 por ciento siempre. Arancel 0 por ciento si la mercancía es de origen estadounidense y tiene certificado T-MEC. Y los costos fijos del pedimento, que son los que decides cuántas veces pagar según el esquema que elijas.

Conviene separar lo que está fijado por ley de lo que depende de tu operación, porque solo lo segundo se puede optimizar. Del lado fijo, el IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana en todo el país, sin excepciones regionales para la importación. El arancel depende del origen: la mercancía de origen estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento bajo el T-MEC siempre que exista certificado de origen, y sin ese documento paga la tasa general aunque califique. Ese detalle vale dinero y se pierde solo por papeleo. Del lado variable está el honorario del agente aduanal, que no está regulado y varía bastante entre proveedores, más la prevalidación y el derecho de trámite. Estos tres son los que se pagan por pedimento. En el régimen simplificado de mensajería el esquema es distinto: se aplica una tasa combinada según origen y valor, sin pedimento formal ni agente aduanal, pero el tope de 2,500 dólares por destinatario limita su uso a volúmenes chicos. Después están los costos por evento, que no tienen tarifa única porque dependen de cómo salga la operación: almacenaje si la mercancía espera, maniobras, y reconocimiento aduanero si el semáforo sale rojo. Nadie honesto te los cotiza de antemano; lo que sí se puede hacer es reducir la probabilidad de que se activen, y eso se logra con documentación consistente.

Cómo elegir según tu etapa

Empieza con mensajería si estás probando el mercado, cambia a consolidación en cuanto compres seguido o a más de un proveedor, y evalúa camión completo cuando un destino jale volumen propio. Casi nadie se salta la etapa intermedia.

El camino que siguen la mayoría de los importadores es bastante consistente, y saberlo evita quemar dinero en la etapa equivocada. Si estás probando el mercado, con muestras o primeras ventas, la mensajería es correcta: no montas nada, aprendes qué se vende y el costo por unidad alto se justifica porque el volumen es bajo. En cuanto empiezas a comprar de forma recurrente, o a más de un proveedor, la consolidación se vuelve la opción obvia, porque es exactamente el escenario para el que existe. Aquí conviene una precaución: tu primera importación formal debe ser deliberadamente conservadora. El IVA se paga al entrar, así que traer de más antes de saber qué rota inmoviliza efectivo en inventario que quizá no se mueva. El camión completo llega después, cuando un destino específico jala volumen suficiente por sí solo. Antes de decidir, resuelve tres cosas que aplican en cualquier esquema: quién será el importador registrado, quién pone la etiqueta en español conforme a la NOM que aplique a tu producto, y a dónde regresan las devoluciones. Esas tres preguntas no dependen del transporte y sin embargo determinan si la operación funciona. BringGo Ship opera bodegas en Laredo y Monterrey, de modo que consolidación, preparación del expediente, etiquetado y entrega nacional quedan en una sola cadena.

  • Carga consolidada: La carga consolidada junta mercancía de uno o varios proveedores para cruzar en una sola importación y repartir los costos fijos.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Cómo puedo enviar productos de Estados Unidos a México?

Por mensajería paquete por paquete, por carga consolidada que cruza en una sola importación formal, o en camión completo. La mensajería sirve para envíos ocasionales, la consolidación es la opción obvia cuando compras seguido, y el camión completo aplica cuando un destino jala volumen propio.

¿Qué impuestos se pagan al importar de EE.UU. a México?

El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana en todo el país. El arancel depende del origen: la mercancía estadounidense entra con 0 por ciento bajo el T-MEC siempre que exista certificado de origen. Sin ese documento paga la tasa general aunque califique, así que vale dinero prepararlo.

¿Por qué conviene consolidar?

Porque los costos fijos de una importación, el honorario del agente aduanal, la prevalidación y el derecho de trámite, se pagan por pedimento y no por tarima. Juntar varios proveedores en un solo cruce reparte esos montos entre mucha más mercancía y baja el costo por unidad de forma notable.

¿Hasta cuánto puedo enviar por mensajería?

El régimen simplificado tiene un tope de 2,500 dólares por destinatario. Por encima de eso se requiere importación formal con pedimento presentado por agente aduanal e importador registrado. Dividir deliberadamente un pedido grande en paquetes chicos para quedar debajo del tope es una conducta que las reglas vigilan.

¿Cuánto tarda un envío de EE.UU. a México?

Un camión bien documentado llega de Laredo a Monterrey en uno o dos días hábiles, porque la distancia son unas horas de camino más el despacho. Lo que alarga el tiempo casi nunca es el trayecto, sino documentación incompleta o inconsistente entre factura, lista de empaque y pedimento.

translations.title: Despacho Aduanal De Estados Unidos A México: Cómo Funciona
translations.excerpt: El despacho no es transporte, es un acto legal. Entender quién lo hace y qué revisa explica casi todos los retrasos que se le achacan al camión.
translations.content:
El despacho aduanal es el proceso por el que la mercancía se legaliza para entrar a México. Lo ejecuta un agente aduanal con patente, que clasifica la mercancía, presenta el pedimento, paga los impuestos y atiende el reconocimiento si el semáforo fiscal marca rojo. Sin despacho, la mercancía no puede circular ni venderse legalmente.

  • Solo un agente aduanal con patente puede presentar el pedimento que legaliza la importación (SAT).
  • El importador debe estar inscrito en el padrón de importadores para operar de forma regular (SAT).
  • El semáforo fiscal determina si la mercancía se libera directamente o pasa a reconocimiento aduanero.
  • El IVA de importación es 16 por ciento y el arancel depende del origen de la mercancía (SAT).
  • La mayoría de las demoras nacen de inconsistencias documentales, no de la distancia ni del transporte.

¿Qué es el despacho aduanal y quién lo hace?

Es el acto legal por el que la mercancía entra formalmente a México. Lo ejecuta un agente aduanal con patente, que es el único autorizado a presentar el pedimento. Ni tú ni tu transportista pueden hacerlo.

El despacho aduanal es el punto donde la mercancía deja de ser un envío y se convierte en una importación. Es un acto legal, no una etapa del transporte, y esa distinción explica por qué se comporta distinto a todo lo demás en la cadena. En el despacho alguien declara ante la autoridad qué entra al país, cómo se clasifica, cuánto vale, de dónde viene y bajo qué régimen, y asume la responsabilidad de que eso sea cierto. La ley reserva ese acto a un agente aduanal con patente. No lo puede hacer el importador por su cuenta, ni el transportista, ni el proveedor en el extranjero. Junto al agente hay una segunda figura obligatoria: el importador, que debe estar inscrito en el padrón de importadores para operar de forma regular y es quien responde ante la autoridad por lo declarado. Estas dos piezas explican una confusión muy común entre empresas extranjeras que quieren vender en México. Puedes organizar tú mismo el transporte, la bodega y la entrega, pero el despacho requiere que exista un agente con patente y un importador registrado. Si no tienes empresa en México, eso se resuelve con un socio que asuma el papel de importador, pero se resuelve antes de que la mercancía se mueva, no cuando ya está en la frontera.

Qué revisa la aduana y qué es el semáforo

Revisa que lo declarado coincida con lo que realmente viene: clasificación, valor, descripción y origen. Al presentar el pedimento el sistema activa el semáforo fiscal, que puede liberar la mercancía o mandarla a reconocimiento físico.

Una vez presentado el pedimento, el sistema aplica el mecanismo de selección automatizada, conocido como semáforo fiscal. Si sale verde, la mercancía se libera y continúa su camino. Si sale rojo, pasa a reconocimiento aduanero: la autoridad revisa físicamente la mercancía para verificar que corresponde a lo declarado. Es importante entender que un rojo no significa que hiciste algo mal; hay un componente aleatorio y también criterios de riesgo. Lo que sí significa es tiempo y maniobras adicionales, normalmente uno o dos días, y por eso ninguna operación seria promete fecha exacta de entrega sin margen. Lo que la autoridad contrasta es la coherencia entre cuatro cosas. La clasificación arancelaria, es decir la fracción con la que se declaró el producto, que determina el impuesto y las regulaciones aplicables. El valor en aduana, que es la base sobre la que se calculan los impuestos y debe coincidir con tu factura. La descripción comercial, que debe permitir identificar la mercancía realmente presentada, y aquí está el detalle que más importa: si la descripción corresponde a lo que físicamente viene, una clasificación equivocada se trata como dato inexacto con una sanción acotada, mientras que si no corresponde el panorama cambia por completo. Y el origen, que decide si aplica el trato preferencial del T-MEC, para lo cual el certificado debe existir.

Cómo evitar que tu carga espere

Prepara el expediente antes de embarcar, cuida que factura, lista de empaque y valor declarado coincidan, clasifica correctamente, ten el certificado de origen listo y etiqueta en origen. El despacho se gana antes de que el camión salga.

Casi todo lo que retrasa una importación se decide antes de que la mercancía se mueva, así que la prevención es documental y no logística. Empieza por la coherencia: factura, lista de empaque y valor declarado deben decir exactamente lo mismo, porque la mayoría de las demoras nace de que un documento contradice a otro. Sigue con la descripción comercial: escríbela de forma que identifique el producto real, evitando términos genéricos, porque una descripción vaga es tanto un riesgo de sanción como una invitación al reconocimiento. Resuelve la clasificación antes de cotizar, no en la frontera, y si tienes duda entre dos fracciones existe la vía de consultar formalmente a la autoridad antes de la operación. Ten el certificado de origen preparado si tu mercancía es estadounidense, porque sin él pagas la tasa general aunque califique para 0 por ciento. Etiqueta en origen conforme a la NOM aplicable, ya que la falta de etiqueta detiene mercancía que por lo demás estaba en regla, y reetiquetar en México cuesta por pieza. Y consolida cuando puedas: menos operaciones significan menos oportunidades de error, además de repartir los costos fijos. Hecho así, el despacho deja de ser el paso incierto de la cadena. BringGo Ship prepara el expediente en su bodega de Laredo antes del cruce, que es exactamente donde este trabajo rinde.
